questions.question: What are blocks and yield in Ruby?
questions.title: Ruby Blocks and Yield
questions.direct_answer: A block is an unnamed chunk of code you pass to a method, written with braces {} (one-liners) or do/end (multi-line): [1,2,3].each { |n| puts n }. A method calls the block with yield — yield runs the block, and yield(value) passes a value to it. The block is what makes iterators like each and map work: the method does the looping, and yield hands each element to the block you provide. You can check block_given? before yielding, and a block turns a method into a custom iterator without writing the loop yourself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know blocks ({}/do-end), yield runs the block and passes values, and block_given? guards yield.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting block_given? (NoMethodError if no block), or confusing yield (calls block) with return.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: A block is an unnamed chunk passed to a method ({}/do-end); yield runs it and passes values. block_given? guards yield. This is how each/map work.

sections.title: Unnamed Code Passed to a Method
sections.content: A block is an unnamed chunk of code you pass to a method, written with braces for one-liners or do/end for multi-line: [1,2,3].each { |n| puts n }. A method calls the block with yield — yield runs the block, and yield(value) passes a value to it. The block is what makes iterators like each and map work: the method does the looping, and yield hands each element to the block you provide. You can check block_given? before yielding to avoid an error when no block is given, and a block turns a method into a custom iterator without writing the loop yourself — that's the whole point of Ruby's iterator style.

sections.title: Method -> yield -> Block
sections.content:
The method loops and yields each value; the block receives it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[method loops] --> Y[yield value]
  Y --> B[block runs with value]
  B --> N[next value or done]
```

sections.title: Blocks and yield
sections.content:
```ruby
# Block with braces (one-liner):
[1, 2, 3].each { |n| puts n }   # prints 1 2 3

# Block with do/end (multi-line):
[1, 2, 3].each do |n|
  puts n * 2
end

# yield in your own method:
def repeat(n)
  n.times { yield }      # run the block n times
end
repeat(3) { puts 'hi' }  # hi hi hi

# yield with a value, and guard with block_given?:
def each_twice(arr)
  return enum_for(:each_twice, arr) unless block_given?
  arr.each { |x| yield x; yield x }   # pass x to the block
end
each_twice([1, 2]) { |v| puts v }   # 1 1 2 2
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting block_given? — yield with no block raises LocalJumpError.
Confusing yield (calls the block) with return (exits the method).
Using {} where do/end reads better for multi-line (style, not a bug).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A block is an unnamed chunk of code passed to a method ({}/do-end).
yield runs the block; yield(value) passes a value to it.
block_given? checks if a block was passed (guard yield against no-block).
Blocks make iterators (each, map) work: the method loops, the block handles each value.
{} for one-liners, do/end for multi-line — convention, not a rule.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A block is an unnamed chunk of code you pass to a method, written with braces for one-liners or do/end for multi-line: one two three dot each with n puts n. A method calls the block with yield — yield runs the block, and yield of value passes a value to it. The block is what makes iterators like each and map work: the method does the looping, and yield hands each element to the block you provide. You can check block given question mark before yielding to avoid an error when no block is given, and a block turns a method into a custom iterator without writing the loop yourself — that's the whole point of Ruby's iterator style. A common mistake is forgetting block given, because yield with no block raises LocalJumpError, and confusing yield, which calls the block, with return, which exits the method.
